In contrast to the housing north of Grand Boulevard, the dwellings along Park Avenue and Jackson, Roosevelt, and Wilson Ways appear to be very poorly-constructed modular housing. These are only permanent trailers, made of plywood, each like the rest, and lacking any sense of design or proportion whatsoever. These homes front on dirt roads which intersect to form a small grid. It seems that this area cannot truly be evaluated as urban design; there is none of the visual nuance of the spaces between building, as say in the campus area, where the houses give shape and content to space, organizing it and forming different arrays of outdoor rooms. This neighborhood of Alviso is simply trailers parked in an open field, a regular pattern of substandard dwellings sited along substandard streets with substandard amenities.
Campus CNRA:
The campus area is most likely the earliest-settled of the seven project areas. The area is bounded on the north and west by the commercially-oriented Santa Clara and South Fourth Streets. Along the eastern boundary (Ninth Street) is located a massive modern concrete parking structure; this parking garage offers a strong contrast to the uses and building types which predominate within the project area.
South of the project area, across San Fernando Street, is the campus of San Jose State University.
Thus, on all four sides, the boundaries of the campus area are well-located so as to enclose the project's similar uses (residential) from the commercial and institutional uses surrounding it.
The area is organized on a street grid pattern; however in this case the area is only one block by five blocks, so its potential monotonous regularity is not experienced in this area. To the contrary the campus area reflects a disorderliness caused by the intrusion of modern commercial and residential structures into an otherwise high-quality residential neighborhood.
The area is characterized by an ample stock of older residences (built as single-family; now often multiple dwellings) constructed in several historical styles. Among these are examples of Queen Anne, Eastlake, Stick Style Bungalow, Spanish, etc. These older dwellings straightforwardly address their streets. But on too many occasions, similarly set back from the street are rectangular, two-and three-story stucco apartment boxes which lack any of the details or grace of the stylized residences. Despite these intrusions, the older residences are still able to convey a sense of their past. The quality of these older buildings and the area's broad representation of historical styles are as fine as any district of comparable age in San Jose. At the least, these residences deserve to be protected from any further intrusions by dis-respectful structures. It seems historical preservation efforts would be warranted in this campus area.
